text.title: Retrieval Cost Audit Failure Modes
text.summary: Six ways a cost audit produces a confidently wrong number, each with the observable symptom and the rule that prevents it.

failure.symptom: The audit reports a small, comfortable number. Nobody can reconcile it with the observed latency or with the context-window pressure the system actually shows.
failure.cause: Instrumentation sat on the vector-store call or the final document read. Routing files, taxonomy reads, index reads and discarded candidates were never counted.
failure.prevention: Count from query arrival to body delivered. On this corpus that moved the number from ~3.3k to ~33k — the leaf read was 10% of the lookup.

failure.symptom: The ledger looks clean and every row is correct. Production cost and quality do not match it in either direction.
failure.cause: Queries were written for the audit rather than sampled from traffic, so they match the retriever's assumptions and skip the shapes that break it.
failure.prevention: Sample from a real log, state the sampling method, and force at least one fact query and one multi-hop query into the set. The published benchmark shows opposite winners on those two shapes.

failure.symptom: Median-cost budgets are set, then a minority of queries blow the context window in production and are treated as unexplained bugs.
failure.cause: A right-skewed distribution was summarised by its mean, so the expensive tail was averaged into invisibility instead of being named.
failure.prevention: Report median and p90, and name the p90 query. The tail case must be a document you can open, not a percentile.

failure.symptom: A new structure wins the audit and is adopted, then the team quietly stops rebuilding the index because the rebuild is unaffordable, and answers drift stale.
failure.cause: Build cost was excluded from the comparison, so a structure with a 7x indexing bill looked cheap on the column that was measured.
failure.prevention: Record `index_build_tokens` separately and amortise it against the corpus change frequency. 654,673 versus 89,215 tokens on one ~56k-token corpus is the difference between nightly rebuilds and a lie.

failure.symptom: Token spend drops sharply after a change; user-visible answer quality drops with it, and the cost dashboard registers the change as a win.
failure.cause: Cost was optimised without a correctness column, so a retriever that returns less of everything scores as an improvement.
failure.prevention: Carry `correct` per row and publish `tokens_per_correct_answer`. Retrieval that fails costs its full tokens and delivers nothing.

failure.symptom: The audit's numbers are round, no instrumentation exists, and the figures are quoted downstream for months as though measured.
failure.cause: Token counts were estimated from character counts or from memory of a pricing page instead of read from usage fields or a local tokenizer.
failure.prevention: If token counts cannot be obtained, do not produce a ledger. An estimate acquires the authority of a measurement the moment it is written down in this format, and the downstream gate cannot tell the difference.
